title: Quarterly framework: Private deployment variance budgeting & sprint commitments
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Objective: Establish a repeatable quarterly planning framework for Private/VPC/on-prem features that explicitly budgets for schedule variance, capacity/cost variance, and operational risk, and ties sprint-level commitments to OKRs. This ticket is the PM artifact that defines the framework, the templates, decision rules, and rollout gating criteria for the upcoming Q1 private deployment tranche.

Context: Over the last two quarters we observed 15-30% schedule slippage across private deployment work (upgrade windows, RBAC, KMS integrations) driven by cross-team dependencies and underestimated verification time in customer environments. Enterprise customers require predictable windows and rollback guarantees. We need a planning cadence that: (1) quantifies expected variance per initiative, (2) reserves sprint buffer capacity, (3) defines go/no-go acceptance gates, and (4) maps each initiative to OKRs and SLA targets.

Scope: Framework applies to all Private/VPC/on-prem initiatives planning for the next two quarters. Includes: capacity/cost variance budgeting, quality/regression buffer, phased rollout commitments, acceptance gates, cross-functional owner matrix, and a lightweight reporting dashboard for PM/Eng/CS. Not in scope: budgeting for non-private hosted API features.

Goals and success metrics: 
- Reduce realized schedule slippage to <= 10% across private initiatives in the next quarter.
- Maintain customer-facing SLA targets during rollouts (latency P99 within 15% of baseline).
- Reduce severity-1 incidents caused by upgrade/compatibility issues by 50% versus previous quarter.
- Capture and publish variance forecast per initiative prior to sprint planning for >90% of private work.

High-level approach: 
1) Variance budgeting: each initiative will have three budget buckets expressed as story points and calendar days: schedule variance (contingency for unknowns), QA/regression buffer (customer environment testing), and operational rollback buffer (post-deploy fixes/mitigation). Templates will default to conservative multipliers based on historical signal (e.g., 20% schedule variance, 15% QA buffer).
2) Sprint commitments and reservation: establish a per-tranche reserved capacity policy that keeps X points per sprint unallocated for emergent issues (default 10%).
3) Acceptance gates: define must-pass criteria per rollout tranche (integration tests in canary env, upgrade verification checklist, readiness confirmation from CS for customer cohorts).
4) OKR mapping: every initiative requires a primary OKR owner and explicit metric ties (e.g., adoption %, incidents per deploy, unit cost delta).
5) Reporting: weekly variance dashboard presented at PM standup and monthly exec readout.

- Draft framework doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PD/Private+Variance+Budgeting+Framework
- Planning template (sheet): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Qx_PlanningTemplatePrivate
- Example tranche plan (customer A): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1abc123-example-tranche-plan
- Prior incident postmortem used for multipliers: https://redwood.atlassian.com/incident/INC-2025-1023

Stakeholders: 
- PM: Liam Chen (assignee)
- Eng leads: Maya Li, Ravi Kapoor
- Reliability: Oscar Fernández
- Customer Success: Priya Nair
- Design: Sophie Morgan (API compatibility UX)

Acceptance criteria: [LIST] 
- [AC1] Framework doc published and reviewed by Eng, Reliability, CS, and Security.
- [AC2] Planning template forked and pre-populated with default multipliers.
- [AC3] Two pilot initiatives scheduled using the template for next sprint cycle.
- [AC4] Weekly variance dashboard populated from pilot and accessible to stakeholders.
- [AC5] Rollout gate checklist created and embedded in release playbook.

Risks: [LIST] 
- Miscalibrated multipliers lead to over-reservation and deprioritization of business-critical work.
- Engineering pushback on buffer reductions due to perceived productivity hit.
- Incomplete telemetry for private environments could hide regressions.

Mitigations: [LIST] 
- Start with conservative defaults and iterate after two tranches; use historical postmortems as calibration.
- Engage eng leads in template design workshop; capture trade-offs explicitly.
- Instrument private deployment flows with lightweight health pings and success markers before Q1 kickoff.

Timeline and milestones: 
- 2026-01-15: Ticket created (this doc).
- 2026-01-20: Stakeholder workshop (done).
- 2026-01-22: Draft framework shared for review (done).
- 2026-01-28: Incorporate feedback, finalize template (target).
- 2026-02-02: Run planning session to schedule pilot initiatives into Cycle 2026-W06.
- 2026-02-12: Pilot tranche ready with rollout gate checklist and dashboard (due date).

Open questions: 
- What is the canonical source of truth for private deployment telemetry (ENG to confirm data wire availability)?
- Do we require explicit product approval from security for every private rollout or only for first-of-kind features?

Next steps: 
- Liam to consolidate feedback from engineering and reliability and update framework by 2026-01-28.
- Maya to validate data wire endpoints and provide ETA by 2026-01-25.
- Priya to nominate two customers for pilot cohorts by 2026-01-26.

comments: 2026-01-20 - Stakeholder workshop notes: strong support for explicit rollback buffer; request from Reliability for automated canary metrics (Oscar).
2026-01-22 - Draft shared: Ravi suggested reducing QA buffer from 20% to 15% for well-understood upgrades; Priya requested CS-run verification checklist for pilot customers.
2026-01-25 - Maya update: data wire endpoints TDB; initial telemetry hooks available in staging by 2026-02-01.
2026-01-27 - Security (Ana Gomes): no blanket approval; security review required for new cryptographic flows but not for pure config changes. Added to decision log.
2026-01-28 - Liam: incorporated feedback from Eng and Security; pushing to finalize template and run planning session on 2026-02-02.
decisions: Use historical incident multipliers as starting defaults (20% schedule, 15% QA, 10% rollback)
Reserve 10% sprint capacity as emergent buffer for private tranches
Security reviews required only for cryptographic/HSM/KMS changes; other features go through standard checklist
risks: Over-reserving capacity reduces throughput for high-priority product work
Insufficient telemetry in private customers hides regressions
Dependencies on external teams (infra/security/ops) create gating delays
mitigations: Iterate multipliers after two pilot tranches and publish adjusted defaults
Implement minimal health pings for private envs before pilots
Create explicit SLAs and hand-off checklist for infra/security tasks tied to each initiative
